Spatial phases, Fourier-basis operators, FFT Hamiltonian actions, phonon forces, photon loss, and the distinction between moving wavefronts and changing spatial moments.

Section 01What is being transported?

A molecular excitation and a cavity photon have very different ways of moving. A photon can connect distant positions through a spatially extended mode. A localized molecular excitation may have little intrinsic mobility. Their hybridization produces polariton bands, but a band dispersion alone does not determine what a lossy, vibrating molecular ensemble will look like after a localized optical excitation.

This paper develops a computational description of that problem beyond a single uniform cavity mode. The molecular positions enter the light–matter coupling through spatial phases. Many photon modes form upper and lower polariton bands, while molecular states outside the optically coupled momentum set provide a dark reservoir. The calculation treats nuclear motion with mean-field Ehrenfest dynamics and incorporates cavity loss. Its main physical questions are how the bath and cavity quality factor change moving wavepackets, apparent velocities, and the crossover between ballistic-like and diffusive-like spreading.

These notes separate three objects that are often called “transport”: the derivative of an ideal band energy, the speed of a feature in a density plot, and the evolution of a spatial moment. They agree only under additional conditions. We derive the multimode Hamiltonian, its Fourier representation, an FFT implementation, and the observables required to interpret the calculation.

The embedded code is a finite-grid, bath-free propagation reference with specified photon loss. It verifies the FFT algebra and reports raw and conditional spatial moments. It is not the paper's full Ehrenfest simulation or a reproduction of its figures.

Primary source: Nano Letters 25, 1617–1622 (2025). The main article is available in the repository. Its separately hosted Supporting Information was not available for inspection in this preparation; numerical implementation details not explicit in the main article are therefore identified as tutorial constructions rather than attributed to that supplement.

Section 02The Hilbert space and the one-excitation basis

Let N two-level molecular excitations occupy positions xn, and let M retained cavity modes have in-plane wavevectors kα. The full electronic–photonic space is

HS=(⨂n=0N−1Hn)⊗(⨂α=1MHc,α).
(1)

We use a zero-based molecular index in the Fourier formulas. A state |n⟩ has molecule n excited and no cavity photons. A state |α⟩ has one photon in mode α and all molecules unexcited. The ordered one-excitation basis is

B1=(|0⟩,|1⟩,…,|N−1⟩;|α=1⟩,…,|α=M⟩).
(2)

The label |0⟩ in this specific basis is molecule 0, not the global ground state. We write that global ground state as |G⟩ throughout. The one-excitation dimension is N+M; including |G⟩ adds one state.

Write a coefficient ket as

|Ψ⟩=∑nxnamp|n⟩+∑αpα|α⟩⟷(|xamp⟩|p⟩)B1.
(3)

The superscript distinguishes the molecular amplitudes xnamp from the spatial coordinates xn. These amplitudes occupy orthogonal molecular and photonic sectors. Their norms add; the scalar sum of a molecular amplitude and a photon amplitude is not itself a physical local amplitude unless a specified measurement mixes the sectors.

Section 03From the microscopic interaction to spatial phases

With vα=ℏgα, an energy-valued Hamiltonian is

H^S=∑nϵnn^n+∑αEαa^α†a^α+∑nα(vαeikαxnσ^n†a^α+vα∗e−ikαxna^α†σ^n).
(4)

The operators n^n=σ^n†σ^n act on molecular factor n, and a^α acts on photon factor α. Their embeddings use identity operators on all remaining factors. The phase expresses the value of a plane-wave mode at the molecule's position. Replacing all phases by one is a long-wavelength approximation that removes the spatial information needed for this transport calculation.

In the one-excitation basis,

[H^S]=(D^xC^C^†D^p),[D^x]nm=ϵnδnm,[D^p]αβ=Eαδαβ,Cnα=vαeikαxn.
(5)

The article's molecular model does not introduce a separate exciton-hopping band. Direct molecular hopping, Peierls-type bath modulation of hopping, and static energetic disorder are distinct extensions. A dense arbitrary coupling matrix would change the algorithmic cost and the physical interpretation of dark-state motion.

Source: the generalized HTC Hamiltonian, Eqs. (1)–(5). The explicit block matrix and complex-coupling convention are derived here.

Section 04Local phonons and the vertical-energy convention

Each molecule couples to an independent collection of harmonic modes:

H^B=∑nν(P^nν22mnν+12mnνωnν2R^nν2),H^SBint=∑nn^n⊗∑νcnνR^nν.
(6)

The reorganization energy is

λn=∑νcnν22mnνωnν2.
(7)

If the bare molecular energy ϵ0 denotes the minimum-to-minimum transition, the diagonal matrix at the undisplaced ground-state bath coordinates contains ϵ0+λ. Completing the excited-state bath squares then lowers its minimum back to ϵ0. Alternatively one can specify the vertical energy directly. The same shift must not be inserted twice.

After the mixed quantum–classical approximation, a trajectory has classical coordinate and momentum kets |R(t)⟩ and |P(t)⟩. Its instantaneous diagonal molecular energies are

ϵ~n(t)=ϵn+∑νcnνRnν(t).
(8)

Even when all molecular parameters are statistically identical, these energies are usually different on a particular trajectory. Momentum eigenstates therefore cease to diagonalize the molecular Hamiltonian on that trajectory. The FFT remains useful for the coupling action because that action retains its spatial phase structure.

Section 05Cavity dispersion and collective coupling

For an ideal planar cavity mode with fixed transverse wavevector, the in-plane photon dispersion can be written

Ep(k)=ℏceffk2+k⊥2=Ec2+(ℏceffk)2.
(9)

Here ceff is the propagation speed used in the cavity model and Ec is its normal-incidence energy. A material refractive index must be included consistently if this formula is being mapped to a specific cavity.

The article includes a frequency-dependent single-molecule coupling proportional to ωk/ωc, together with a dipole–polarization projection. A convenient notation is

vk=v0Ep(k)Eccos⁡θ,Vk=Nvk.
(10)

The angle θ is the molecular transition-dipole projection on the mode polarization. It should not automatically be identified with the photon propagation angle. A model for rotating polarization vectors or orientational disorder needs its own geometry.

The collective matrix element Vk, not vk, appears in a normalized bright-state block. At a resonance with a single bright mode, the energy splitting is 2|Vk|. Comparing different system sizes at fixed vk changes this splitting; comparing at fixed Vk does not.

Section 06The discrete Fourier basis

Take equally spaced positions xn=na in a periodic domain of length ℓ=Na. Allowed grid momenta are kq=2πq/ℓ, interpreted modulo the grid size. Define normalized molecular momentum states

|q⟩x=1N∑n=0N−1ei2πqn/N|n⟩,Fqn=1Ne−i2πqn/N.
(11)

The coordinate transform is |x~⟩=F^|xamp⟩. The inverse is |xamp⟩=F^†|x~⟩. Orthogonality follows from a finite geometric series:

∑n=0N−1ei2π(q−q′)n/N=Nδqq′,F^†F^=I^.
(12)

For N=4, in the ordered site basis (|0⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩,|3⟩),

[F^]=12(11111−i−1i1−11−11i−1−i).
(13)

The normalization is not cosmetic. Using a library FFT without its normalization factors changes the collective coupling by a factor of N. The reference code uses norm="ortho" for both forward and inverse transforms.

Section 07An explicit six-state Fourier-coupled example

Take four molecular sites but retain only two photon modes, at Fourier bins q=0,1. Let both have the same real collective coupling V. In the ordered site rows and photon columns,

[C^]=V2(111i1−11−i).
(14)

The columns are orthogonal, so C^†C^=V2I^2. Transform only the molecular block with F^. In the basis (|q=0⟩x,|q=1⟩x,|q=2⟩x,|q=3⟩x;|p0⟩,|p1⟩),

[H^]=(ϵ000V00ϵ000V00ϵ000000ϵ00V000Ep000V000Ep1).
(15)

There are two bright two-by-two blocks and two uncoupled molecular momentum states. The latter are dark with respect to the retained photon set, not because their local molecular transition dipoles have vanished. Adding more photon modes changes which molecular momenta are bright.

This example also explains why a single uniform bright state is insufficient for transport. A spatial wavepacket requires a superposition of many momenta; the relative phase between those momenta carries its position and motion.

Section 08Bright polariton bands and the remaining dark subspace

For a retained momentum k, the bright block in (|k⟩x,|k⟩p) is

[H^k]=(ϵVkVk∗Ep(k)).
(16)

Let δk=Ep(k)−ϵ and Δk=δk2+4|Vk|2. The band energies are

E±(k)=ϵ+Ep(k)2±Δk2.
(17)

For the lower polariton, the photon and molecular weights are

|C−(k)|2=12(1−δkΔk),|X−(k)|2=1−|C−(k)|2.
(18)

For the upper branch they are interchanged. At large positive detuning the lower branch is mostly molecular; at large negative detuning it is mostly photonic. This limit is a reliable way to catch a reversed mixing-angle convention.

When the retained photon columns are orthogonal and nonzero, their rank is M, and there are N−M molecular dark states. More generally the count is N−rankC^. Degenerate labels or zero couplings must not be counted as independent bright channels.

Section 09Deriving the ideal group velocity

For a narrow wavepacket on an isolated band, the ideal group velocity is

v±(k)=1ℏdE±(k)dk.
(19)

This result follows by Taylor expanding the phase of a Fourier packet about k0: E(k)≃E(k0)+E′(k0)(k−k0). The linear term translates the envelope by E′(k0)t/ℏ; the quadratic term changes its width.

If ϵ is constant, differentiation of the polariton eigenvalue gives

dE−(k)dk=|C−(k)|2Ep′(k)−2Re[Vk∗Vk′]Δk.
(20)

For a momentum-independent coupling the second term vanishes and the usual photon-fraction-weighted velocity follows. For Vk∝Ep(k) with fixed phase and orientation,

Vk′=VkEp′(k)2Ep(k),dE−dk=|C−|2Ep′−|Vk|2Ep′EpΔk.
(21)

The bare photon derivative is Ep′=(ℏceff)2k/Ep. Ignoring the derivative of the coupling is an approximation, not an identity. A dispersive molecular band would add |X−|2ϵ′(k) as well.

Section 10Wavepacket motion from the dispersion expansion

A lower-polariton packet can be prepared as

|Ψ(0)⟩=∑q∈QAqe−ikqx0|−,q⟩,∑q|Aq|2=1,
(22)

with a Gaussian momentum envelope Aq. For an isolated band without loss,

|Ψ(t)⟩=∑qAqe−ikqx0e−iE−(kq)t/ℏ|−,q⟩.
(23)

Expanding E−(k) through second order around the packet center shows separately the center velocity and dispersive broadening. A very broad momentum packet cannot be assigned one group velocity without specifying how the velocity is averaged or measured.

A molecular-site excitation, a photon packet, and a branch-filtered polariton packet are different initial conditions. A localized molecule generally excites both polariton branches and dark components. A narrow photon packet can emphasize one band after spectral selection, but not simply by naming it “LP” without applying the appropriate projection.

The reference code prepares a lower-band wavepacket by constructing and combining the normalized eigenvectors at every retained momentum. It thereby separates band propagation from an arbitrary mixture of branches.

Section 11Replacing a dense coupling matrix by FFTs

Let S^ be the N×M selection matrix that inserts retained photon-mode amplitudes into their corresponding Fourier bins. With V^=diag(Vα),

C^=F^†S^V^,C^†=V^†S^†F^.
(24)

Applying the full Hamiltonian to a ket then requires

|yx⟩=D^x|xamp⟩+F^†S^V^|p⟩,|yp⟩=D^p|p⟩+V^†S^†F^|xamp⟩.
(25)

In code, multiply photon amplitudes by Vα, put them into a zero-filled length-N momentum array, and apply the inverse FFT. For the opposite direction, FFT the molecular amplitudes, select the retained bins, and multiply by Vα∗. The diagonal energy products are ordinary elementwise operations.

This costs O(Nlog⁡N+M) rather than a generic O(NM) coupling multiplication. The FFT speedup does not assume the nuclear trajectory is translationally invariant. It assumes the coupling geometry has the required Fourier form.

A sequence of molecular positions that is not a uniform grid, an arbitrary set of incommensurate photon wavevectors, or arbitrary nonseparable site–mode couplings does not fit this exact construction. Such cases require a different multiplication strategy; silently rounding their wavevectors to FFT bins changes the model.

Section 12Checking every normalization with a single momentum state

Prepare |xamp⟩=|q0⟩x, with q0 among the retained modes. Orthogonality gives

F^|q0⟩x=|q0⟩coordinate,C^†|q0⟩x=Vq0∗|pq0⟩.
(26)

Only one photon mode should receive an amplitude, and the magnitude must be the collective coupling |Vq0|. A dark momentum not among the retained bins must produce zero photon amplitude.

For a random complex ket, compare the FFT result with a separately built dense matrix. Test ∥H^FFT|Ψ⟩−H^dense|Ψ⟩∥, and also check ⟨u|H^|v⟩=⟨v|H^|u⟩∗. These tests catch phase signs, FFT-bin order, conjugation, and normalization errors before any dynamics is run.

The teaching script performs both tests. A Fourier acceleration should be exact up to floating-point error for the same finite matrix; it should not be validated only by a visually similar final wavepacket.

Section 13Nuclear dynamics in the mean-field Ehrenfest approximation

For a normalized pure electronic–photonic state and classical nuclei, the mean-field energy is

EMF(R,P,Ψ)=HB(R,P)+⟨Ψ|H^S(R)|Ψ⟩.
(27)

Hamilton's equations for the nuclear variables give

R˙nν=Pnνmnν,P˙nν=−mnνωnν2Rnν−cnν⟨Ψ|n^n|Ψ⟩.
(28)

The quantum ket evolves under the instantaneous Hamiltonian. For the one-excitation basis, ⟨n^n⟩=|xnamp|2. The nuclear force therefore depends on where the molecular part of the wavepacket is located.

In a mixed-state mean-field formulation, replace the expectation by Tr(n^nρ^S). In a quantum-jump trajectory formulation, a jump may change the force surface and the subsequent nuclear history. A no-jump state must not be normalized or left unnormalized in the force formula without specifying which ensemble interpretation is being used.

Ehrenfest dynamics is not exact quantum nuclear dynamics. It can miss branching of nuclear wavepackets, detailed-balance behavior, and correlations important in strong-coupling or long-time regimes. The FFT implementation accelerates its quantum-state update; it does not remove those physical limitations.

Source: the article's choice of mean-field Ehrenfest dynamics and the Hamiltonian. The variational derivation and force-convention discussion are tutorial explanations.

Section 14Thermal Wigner sampling and the bath spectrum

For a harmonic mode initially thermal on the ground-state potential, the Wigner distribution is Gaussian with zero means and variances

⟨R2⟩W=ℏ2mωcoth⁡βℏω2,⟨P2⟩W=mℏω2coth⁡βℏω2,⟨RP⟩W=0.
(29)

The high-temperature limit recovers ⟨R2⟩=kBT/(mω2) and ⟨P2⟩=mkBT. The zero-temperature limit retains the zero-point widths. Replacing these widths by classical thermal widths is an additional approximation.

For the convention

J(ω)=π2∑νcν2mνωνδ(ω−ων),λ=1π∫0∞J(ω)ωdω,
(30)

one common Drude form is J(ω)=2λγω/(ω2+γ2). Discretization must reproduce both the intended correlation time and the reorganization energy. Increasing the number of bath modes is a different convergence test from increasing the number of trajectories.

Sampling independent baths means independent random variables for different molecular sites. Reusing the same random trace on every molecule replaces local disorder by a fully correlated fluctuation and strongly changes bright–dark scattering.

Section 15How local baths scatter momentum

In the molecular momentum basis, the fluctuation operator has matrix elements

x⟨q|H^SBint|q′⟩x=1N∑nei(kq′−kq)xnB^n.
(31)

Thus a diagonal operator in the site basis is generally off diagonal in momentum. It can scatter a bright molecular momentum into another bright momentum or into a dark momentum not matched by a retained photon mode.

If every site instead experienced exactly the same operator B^, the sum would give B^δqq′, with no momentum scattering. This proves directly why independent local environments cannot be replaced by one collective bath when transport and dark-state transfer are the observables of interest.

For identical independent baths, a matrix element between normalized delocalized states typically has a variance decreasing with N, but there are many final dark states. The sum over final-state channels can remain finite. A reduced diagonal fluctuation of an individual bright state therefore does not imply that all bath-induced transport changes disappear at large N.

Section 16Quality factor, linewidth, and photon lifetime

Let Γα be the photon population-decay energy width, so that κα=Γα/ℏ is a rate. For a mode at energy Eα, define

Qα=EαΓα,τα=1κα=ℏQαEα.
(32)

Its probability decays as e−t/τα, and its amplitude decays as e−t/(2τα). The factor of two is important when converting an optical amplitude linewidth into a population lifetime.

A mode-resolved loss model has jump operators

L^α=κα|G⟩⟨α|,dρ^dt=−iℏ[H^,ρ^]+∑α(L^αρ^L^α†−12{L^α†L^α,ρ^}).
(33)

Independent mode-resolved leakage and coherent leakage into a common unresolved output channel are not automatically the same model. Here we explicitly use mode-resolved loss. The one-excitation survival satisfies

dPsurvdt=−∑ακαραα,ρGG=1−Psurv
(34)

for a normalized initial one-excitation state and no re-excitation. A loss width alone does not change the Hermitian bare band derivative; it changes survival, coherence, and the weights of components observed at later times.

Section 17When a non-Hermitian ket is an exact reduced calculation

For a fixed finite system with loss only from the one-excitation sector to an inert ground state, the surviving block evolves under

H^eff=H^1−iℏ2∑ακα|α⟩⟨α|.
(35)

Starting from one pure excitation, solve iℏ∂t|ψ⟩=H^eff|ψ⟩ without renormalizing. Then

ρ^(t)=|ψ(t)⟩⟨ψ(t)|+[1−⟨ψ(t)|ψ(t)⟩]|G⟩⟨G|
(36)

is the exact finite-system density operator for that model. The omitted jumps all end in the same inert state and do not feed the excited block. This is why an unnormalized ket is sufficient for the teaching demo.

The conclusion is narrower than “non-Hermitian propagation is always equivalent to Lindblad.” It fails when jumps feed other retained excited states, when a pulse subsequently re-excites the system, or when the bath trajectory after a jump matters to the requested observable. It also does not make an Ehrenfest treatment of coupled nuclei exact.

The ground state should not be assigned an arbitrary position in a spatial moment and counted as an excitation remaining at that position. Lost probability belongs to a separate sector of the measurement.

Section 18Defining a real-space density for both sectors

The molecular density is directly Px(n)=|xnamp|2. For photon modes, define a grid wavefunction by zero-padding the retained modes and inverse transforming:

|pgrid⟩=F^†S^|p⟩,Pp(n)=|pngrid|2.
(37)

Because S^†S^=I^M and F^ is unitary,

∑nPp(n)=⟨p|p⟩,P(n)=Px(n)+Pp(n),∑nP(n)=Psurv.
(38)

This corresponds to a block-diagonal measurement that resolves excitation location but does not coherently mix molecular and photon sectors. There is no direct term 2Re(xnamp∗pngrid) in this measurement. A different observable, such as a polarization–field correlation, can contain cross-sector coherence but must be defined explicitly.

Within a molecular density expressed in upper- and lower-band components, cross terms can occur because both components project onto the same molecular sector. “Interference” therefore depends on the observable and the decomposition; it should not be added to a probability formula by analogy with scalar waves alone.

Section 19Position operators and a finite-grid subtlety

In the molecular site basis, the position operator is X^x=diag(x0,…,xN−1). The photon position measurement on the retained-mode space is obtained by projection:

X^p=S^†F^X^xF^†S^.
(39)

For the second moment, however, the corresponding projected operator is

X^p,2=S^†F^X^x2F^†S^,
(40)

which need not equal X^p2 when only a subset of modes is retained. Squaring a projected position matrix is not the same as projecting the full-grid second-moment measurement. Computing moments from Pp(n) automatically uses the latter consistent definition.

Periodic coordinates introduce a further issue. A packet crossing the edge of the numerical box can make a Cartesian mean or variance jump. Use a large enough box to avoid wraparound over the analysis window, or define an unwrapped/circular statistic appropriate to the question. The reference demo reports moments only over a window chosen to keep the packet away from the boundary.

Section 20Band-resolved localized states form a frame

For a chosen polariton band and retained momentum set Q, define

|±,n⟩=1N∑q∈Qe−ikqxn|±,q⟩.
(41)

When M<N, these states are not an orthonormal position basis:

⟨±,n|±,m⟩=1N∑q∈Qeikq(xn−xm),⟨±,n|±,n⟩=MN.
(42)

Nevertheless they satisfy a useful completeness relation on the retained band,

∑n|±,n⟩⟨±,n|=Π^±.
(43)

Thus the nonnegative quantities |⟨±,n|Ψ⟩|2 sum to the band's population. This is a tight-frame representation, not a set of unit-normalized mutually exclusive position eigenstates. Multiplying each frame ket by N/M and continuing to sum its squared overlaps without compensating weights would overcount the population.

Source: the localized polariton construction around Eq. (6). The frame normalization and its interpretation are derived explicitly here.

Section 21Raw displacement, conditional displacement, and variance

Fix the initial packet center xinit. Define the unnormalized second displacement moment

M2raw(t)=∑n(xn−xinit)2P(n,t).
(44)

If the surviving excitation probability is nonzero, the conditional moment is

M2cond(t)=M2raw(t)Psurv(t).
(45)

The conditional center and central variance are

x¯(t)=∑nxnP(n,t)Psurv(t),σx2(t)=∑n[xn−x¯(t)]2P(n,t)Psurv(t).
(46)

These quantities satisfy

M2cond(t)=σx2(t)+[x¯(t)−xinit]2.
(47)

A narrow packet translating at constant speed has a growing second displacement moment even if its central variance does not grow. Calling that “diffusion” would conflate translation with spreading. The article's transient displacement discussion is best read alongside the corresponding density maps and surviving populations.

The origin of the moment, its normalization, and the treatment of loss must all be stated before comparing simulations. Two codes can report different “MSDs” while propagating identical wavefunctions.

Section 22Why loss can make an MSD decrease without reversing motion

Consider a sharply localized packet moving ballistically at speed v with uniform survival e−κt. Then

M2cond=v2t2,M2raw=e−κtv2t2.
(48)

Differentiate the raw moment:

dM2rawdt=v2e−κtt(2−κt).
(49)

It reaches a maximum at t=2/κ, then decreases even though every surviving packet continues forward. This elementary counterexample shows why a declining raw moment is not evidence that the surviving polariton has reversed its velocity.

More generally,

dln⁡M2rawdln⁡t=dln⁡Psurvdln⁡t+dln⁡M2conddln⁡t
(50)

when the quantities are positive. A log–log exponent extracted from the raw moment contains a survival contribution. For a finite-width initial packet, subtracting the initial width or analyzing central variance may be appropriate, but the definition must remain consistent through the fit.

Section 23Ballistic and diffusive limits from a velocity correlation

For a stationary zero-mean velocity process, the displacement is Δx(t)=∫0tv(s)ds. Therefore

⟨Δx(t)2⟩=2∫0t(t−τ)Cv(τ)dτ,Cv(τ)=⟨v(τ)v(0)⟩.
(51)

A constant velocity correlation gives quadratic, ballistic growth. A rapidly decaying integrable correlation gives linear growth at long times, with D=∫0∞Cv(τ)dτ.

For a simple persistent walker that flips between velocities ±v0 at rate ν, Cv(τ)=v02e−2ντ. Integration gives

⟨Δx2⟩=v02ν[t−1−e−2νt2ν].
(52)

Expanding the exponential at short times yields v02t2. At long times the expression becomes 2Dt plus a constant, with D=v02/(2ν). This is a teaching model for how loss of directional memory changes a transport exponent. It is not a microscopic derivation of the molecular bath's scattering rate in the article.

A fitted exponent between one and two over a finite interval can describe a crossover without defining a new asymptotic transport law. The observation window, packet preparation, finite box, and loss must be checked first.

Section 24Extracting a front velocity from a density map

A front velocity is obtained by selecting a feature, such as the outer maximum of a band-resolved density, and fitting its position versus time. This feature can move differently from the probability-weighted center, especially when the packet splits into branches, transfers into dark states, or loses its photonic component.

A reproducible procedure is to specify the density being analyzed, the branch or spatial side being tracked, the minimum signal threshold, the time window, and the fit uncertainty. The same rule should be applied to every bath strength or quality factor. A late-time peak that switches from one branch to another should not be joined into one trajectory without explanation.

The ideal band derivative supplies a reference velocity. A reduced fitted front velocity can result from dynamical dressing, scattering, transfer between components with different velocities, and survival selection. Distinguishing these mechanisms requires the accompanying populations and density evolution, not just one slope.

This is the sense in which the article's dynamical velocity renormalization is richer than diagonalizing a static two-by-two matrix. The simulation tracks a time-dependent packet in a dissipative many-state system.

Section 25How a flat dark band can acquire a broad spatial population

Without direct molecular hopping, an ideal dark molecular momentum state has flat energy and zero band derivative. Yet the dark-state density can spread across many sites in a transport simulation. There is no contradiction if mobile bright polaritons deposit population into the dark subspace at different positions and times.

A schematic source equation makes the distinction explicit:

∂tPD(x,t)=SB→D(x,t)−SD→B(x,t)−κDPD(x,t).
(53)

Even with no intrinsic spatial derivative term for PD, a moving source SB→D(x,t) creates a broad dark-state distribution. Its width records where mobile states transferred their excitation; it does not prove that the uncoupled dark eigenstates possess a nonzero group velocity.

Conversely, bath-mediated return from dark to bright sectors can enable further motion. A reduced kinetic picture may be useful after its rates are justified, but it is not automatically equivalent to coherent Ehrenfest dynamics.

Source: the article's population-resolved transport discussion and Fig. 3. The source-equation interpretation is a tutorial model for distinguishing transfer-generated spatial structure from intrinsic dark-band velocity.

Section 26A reading guide to the reported results

The numerical results compare phonon coupling strengths, cavity quality factors, and initial polariton character. The main qualitative findings are slower dynamical propagation with stronger environmental effects, pronounced lifetime-dependent changes in transient spatial moments, and a crossover in the observed spreading behavior. These are numerical results for the modeled cavity–exciton ensemble, not a universal formula connecting a quality factor to one velocity.

Figure in the main article Main diagnostic Useful interpretation check
Fig. 1 Moving polariton distributions and apparent velocities Compare to the ideal dispersion, not only to another trajectory
Fig. 2 Transient mean-square displacement and quality factor Separate survival loss from conditional spreading
Fig. 3 Bright, dark, and ground-state population behavior Identify where excitation is transferred or lost
Fig. 4 Different photon fractions and ballistic/diffusive-like windows State the fit interval and the prepared momentum packet

The model uses a large molecular ensemble and a restricted photon-mode set to make direct transport simulation feasible. The paper's parameter choices should be consulted when reproducing a particular panel. The small demo attached here intentionally does not claim agreement with those bath-dependent figures.

One particularly valuable comparison is between the ideal dE/dk curve, a front-position fit, and the conditional second moment. Disagreement among them is often the physics to understand, not automatically a numerical failure.

Source: Figs. 1–2, Fig. 3, and Fig. 4 and conclusions.

Section 27A band-scale and lifetime calculator

The calculator below uses a flat exciton band and an ideal photon dispersion. It reports the lower-polariton composition and group velocity, including the derivative of the coupling when the square-root dispersion option is selected. It also reports the cavity lifetime implied by the stated definition of Q. It predicts neither the article's bath-renormalized velocity nor a diffusion coefficient.

A negative wavevector reverses the velocity for this inversion-symmetric model. At k=0, the derivative of the even photon dispersion vanishes. A large photonic fraction at normal incidence therefore does not by itself imply a nonzero in-plane group velocity.

Section 28The numerical reference and what it tests

The downloadable teaching code uses a normalized discrete Fourier transform, constructs a multimode Hamiltonian, and compares dense and FFT actions on random complex kets. It checks bright/dark momentum selection, verifies the group-velocity derivative by finite differences, and propagates a finite lower-band packet with mode-resolved photon loss.

python polariton_transport_teaching.py --test
python polariton_transport_teaching.py --demo --output transport_demo.csv

The demo outputs surviving population, photon and molecular populations, the conditional center, raw second displacement moment, conditional second displacement moment, and central variance. These columns are intentionally separate. It also records the domain and propagation window so that boundary contamination can be assessed.

There are no sampled nuclear bath trajectories in this script. It should be used as a normalization and observable-definition reference before adding the significantly more involved Ehrenfest dynamics. The article's bath-dependent transport results require that additional dynamics and its convergence tests.

Section 29Twelve worked checks

1. Count bright and dark states for four sites and two independent modes.
The one-excitation dimension is 4+2=6. The coupling matrix has rank two, so two molecular combinations are bright and two are dark. Each bright molecular combination hybridizes with one photon, producing four polariton eigenstates. Adding the ground state gives seven states in total.
2. Verify one column of the four-site coupling matrix.
For q=1, the phase column is (1,i,−1,−i)T. Its squared norm is four. Multiplying by V/2 gives norm |V|, exactly the collective coupling. The inner product with the q=0 column is proportional to 1+i−1−i=0.
3. Explain why a missing FFT normalization changes the Rabi splitting.
A normalized bright ket has site amplitudes of magnitude 1/N. Summing its coupling to all sites gives Nv/N=Nv=V. A transform convention that replaces this normalized sum by an unscaled sum inserts an extra N. The resulting apparent splitting is wrong even though the code may remain numerically stable.
4. Find the lower-polariton photon weight far above resonance.
For δ=Ep−ϵ≫|V|, expand Δ=δ1+4|V|2/δ2. Then |C−|2≈|V|2/δ2, which tends to zero. The lower branch is mostly molecular. A formula giving a photon weight near one in this limit has exchanged the branches or detuning sign.
5. Calculate a cavity lifetime from an energy linewidth.
Take Ec=2 eV and Q=500. The energy width is Γ=Ec/Q=0.004 eV. Using ℏ=0.0006582119569 eV·ps gives a population lifetime τ=0.16455 ps. The isolated photon amplitude envelope has a decay time 2τ, not τ/2.
6. Distinguish translation from spreading.
A rigid packet with initial variance σ02 and center xinit+vt has σx2(t)=σ02, while M2cond(t)=σ02+v2t2. Quadratic growth of the displacement moment does not require the packet to broaden.
7. Find the time at which a lossy ballistic raw moment peaks.
For an initially pointlike packet, M2raw=v2t2e−κt. Its derivative vanishes at t=0 and t=2/κ. The latter is the maximum. With a 100 fs survival lifetime it peaks at 200 fs even though the conditional center continues to move at speed v.
8. Show that a spatially uniform bath cannot scatter molecular momentum.
Set every B^n=B^. The Fourier matrix element becomes B^N−1∑nei(kq′−kq)xn=B^δqq′. Independent local baths do not permit this simplification, so they can transfer population among momentum and dark sectors.
9. Check the normalization of a band-localized frame ket.
The ket is a sum of M orthonormal momentum eigenstates with amplitude 1/N. Its norm squared is M/N. Summing the outer products over the N sites restores the band projector because the lattice phase sum supplies Nδqq′. Individual nonunit norm does not prevent a correct frame resolution.
10. Derive the diffusive limit of the persistent-walker model.
For t≫1/(2ν), the exponential in the exact moment is negligible. The leading term is v02t/ν=2Dt, hence D=v02/(2ν). At short times the linear terms cancel and the remaining leading term is v02t2.
11. Can a dark population become broad without a dark-state group velocity?
Yes. A moving bright packet can transfer population into dark states at successive locations. Integrating a moving source SB→D(x,t) creates a broad dark distribution even if the dark evolution contains no spatial transport term. The spatial width of a reservoir is not itself a measurement of its isolated band derivative.
12. What must be checked before claiming diffusion from a fitted exponent?
Specify whether the moment is raw or conditioned on survival, remove or account for center translation and initial width, avoid periodic wraparound, test the fit-window dependence, converge trajectories and bath discretization, and inspect the density map. A finite-window slope near one is suggestive but does not by itself establish an asymptotic diffusion coefficient.

Section 30What to validate before scaling the calculation

Begin with dense/FFT agreement and momentum-selection tests. Next set the bath and loss to zero and check norm conservation, packet translation, and agreement between the band derivative and a narrow-packet center velocity. Introduce loss without a bath and verify both the survival equation and the raw–conditional moment identity. Only then add nuclear forces, thermal sampling, and independent local baths.

Converge the spatial lattice and photon momentum cutoff separately. A larger molecular grid changes the real-space box or spacing depending on what is held fixed; a larger photon-mode set changes the represented optical bandwidth and dark-state count. Increasing both together without recording these choices can obscure the origin of a change in transport.

For a bath calculation, report the spectral density, its discretization, initial-state preparation, mean-field force convention, loss model, timestep, trajectory count, and the averaging order for conditional observables. Averaging a conditional moment separately over trajectories is generally not the same as conditioning the ensemble-averaged density.

Section 31Connections to spectroscopy and collective dynamics

The linear-spectroscopy paper demonstrates the value of structured Hamiltonian actions in a single-mode ensemble. Here the structure is Fourier rather than a single star. The nonlinear-spectroscopy paper shows how the same discipline extends to optical operators, multiple excitation manifolds, and trajectory branches.

Together these examples illustrate a practical principle: choose the basis in which each operation is simplest, and transform only when an operation requires it. The molecular basis is natural for local baths and spatial probabilities; the momentum basis is natural for uniform cavity couplings and ideal bands. Neither basis alone contains the complete physical interpretation of a dissipative transport experiment.
